fetched_contents.text: Treatment with LABA versus LAMA for stable COPD: a systematic review and meta-analysis Abstract Background Inhaled bronchodilators including long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) and long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) play a central role in the treatment of stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). However, it is still unclear whether LABA or LAMA should be used for the initial treatment. Therefore, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy and safety of LABA versus LAMA in patients with stable COPD. Methods We searched relevant randomized control trials (RCTs) with a period of treatment of at least 12 weeks and analyzed the exacerbations, quality of life, dyspnea score, lung function and adverse events as the outcomes of interest. Results We carefully excluded unblinded data and identified a total of 19 RCTs (N = 28,211). LAMA significantly decreased the exacerbations compared to LABA (OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.98; P = 0.02). In St George’s Respiratory Questionnaire and transitional dyspnoea index score, there were no differences between LABA and LAMA treatment. Compared to LABA, there was a small but significant increase in the trough FEV1 after LAMA treatment (Mean difference 0.02, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.03, P = 0.0006). In the safety components, there was no difference in the serious adverse events between LABA and LAMA. However, LAMA showed a significantly lower incidence of total adverse events compared to LABA (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.86 to 0.98; P = 0.02). Conclusion Treatment with LAMA in stable COPD provided a significantly lower incidence of exacerbation and non-serious adverse events, and a higher trough FEV1 compared to LABA. The most common symptoms include dyspnea, cough and sputum production, with the symptoms worsening during exacerbations. For the treatment of stable COPD patients, inhaled bronchodilators play a central role in reducing symptoms and exacerbations. Regular daily use of either a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) or long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) has been shown to improve the lung function, dyspnea and health status and reduce exacerbations [2–4]. In addition, these bronchodilators improve exercise performance [5, 6]. Currently available LAMA comprises tiotropium, glycopyrronium, aclidinium and umeclidinium and LABA includes salmeterol, formoterol, indacaterol, vilanterol and olodaterol. Now, either LABA or LAMA is first used for the treatment of patients with stable COPD. According to the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) report 2019, there is no mention which bronchodilator, LABA or LAMA, is superior for the initial relief of the symptoms in the GOLD grade group A and B patients [7]. On the other hand, in group C and D patients that have experienced exacerbations of COPD, LAMA is more often recommended as a single initial therapy than LABA. However, this is only due to two head-to-head comparison studies which showed the superiority of tiotropium to salmeterol or indacaterol in preventing exacerbations [8, 9]. Therefore, it remains unclear which bronchodilator, LABA or LAMA, is more suitable for the initial treatment of stable COPD. Until now, several systematic reviews have been reported for comparison between LABA and LAMA for the treatment of patients with stable COPD [10–13]. However, these reviews mainly compared tiotropium with salmeterol or indacaterol in up to six different studies. In the latest review, Chen, et al. evaluated 16 studies that included LABA (salmeterol, formoterol, indacaterol and olodaterol) and LAMA (tiotropium, glycopyrronium, aclidinium and umeclidinium), and showed the superiority of LAMA over LABA in the prevention of COPD exacerbation and fewer adverse events [13]. However, the analysis contained open labeled-tiotropium group or unblinded studies which could reduce the accuracy of the meta-analysis. Therefore, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis, not only excluding the unblinded data, but also adding several new trials. To clarify whether LABA or LAMA is more beneficial for the initial treatment of patients with stable COPD, we searched relevant randomized control clinical trials and evaluated the efficacy and safety of LABA versus LAMA by measuring exacerbations, quality of life, dyspnea score, lung function and adverse events. Methods Search strategy and eligibility criteria This systematic review and the meta-analysis were conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidance [14]. The study protocol was registered in the PROSPERO database (www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/; registration number: CRD42019144764). We firstly set outcomes from clinical importance and then performed a systematic research to acquire literature. We searched and identified randomized controlled trials in MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Pubmed and EMBASE databases on November 2018, using the search strategy provided in the on-line supplement. We also conducted a search of ClinicalTrials.gov (www.ClinicalTrials.gov). Only publications described in English were considered. As the inclusion criteria, participants had a diagnosis of stable COPD according to the GOLD report’s diagnostic criteria. Randomized controlled trials comparing LABA and LAMA were included if they evaluated any of our outcomes of interest with at least 12 weeks of treatment duration. fetched_contents.text: Comparisons of exacerbations and mortality among regular inhaled therapies for patients with stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: Systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis Abstract Background Although exacerbation and mortality are the most important clinical outcomes of stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), the drug classes that are the most efficacious in reducing exacerbation and mortality among all possible inhaled drugs have not been determined. Methods and findings We performed a systematic review (SR) and Bayesian network meta-analysis (NMA). We searched Medline, EMBASE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, ClinicalTrials.gov, the European Union Clinical Trials Register, and the official websites of pharmaceutical companies (from inception to July 9, 2019). The eligibility criteria were as follows: (1) parallel-design randomized controlled trials (RCTs); (2) adults with stable COPD; (3) comparisons among long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMAs), long-acting beta-agonists (LABAs), inhaled corticosteroids (ICSs), combined treatment (ICS/LAMA/LABA, LAMA/LABA, or ICS/LABA), or a placebo; and (4) study duration ≥ 12 weeks. This study was prospectively registered in International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; CRD42017069087). In total, 219 trials involving 228,710 patients were included. Compared with placebo, all drug classes significantly reduced the total exacerbations and moderate to severe exacerbations. ICS/LAMA/LABA was the most efficacious treatment for reducing the exacerbation risk (odds ratio [OR] = 0.57; 95% credible interval [CrI] 0.50–0.64; posterior probability of OR > 1 [P(OR > 1)] < 0.001). In addition, in contrast to the other drug classes, ICS/LAMA/LABA and ICS/LABA were associated with a significantly higher probability of reducing mortality than placebo (OR = 0.74, 95% CrI 0.59–0.93, P[OR > 1] = 0.004; and OR = 0.86, 95% CrI 0.76–0.98, P[OR > 1] = 0.015, respectively). The results minimally changed, even in various sensitivity and covariate-adjusted meta-regression analyses. ICS/LAMA/LABA tended to lower the risk of cardiovascular mortality but did not show significant results. ICS/LAMA/LABA increased the probability of pneumonia (OR for triple therapy = 1.56; 95% CrI 1.19–2.03; P[OR > 1] = 1.000). The main limitation is that there were few RCTs including only less symptomatic patients or patients at a low risk. Conclusions These findings suggest that triple therapy can potentially be the best option for stable COPD patients in terms of reducing exacerbation and all-cause mortality. ---------------------------------------- In this systematic review and network meta-analysis, Chang-Hoon Lee and colleagues compare efficacy and safety of drugs and drug combinations for treating COPD. Author summary Why was this study done? * Pharmacologic inhaled therapies are cornerstones for treating patients with stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) to improve their health condition and reduce the future risk of exacerbation and mortality while minimizing significant drug-related adverse events. However, the best inhaled therapy for reducing exacerbation, mortality, and adverse events is unknown. * As previous evidence is not enough to determine which inhaled therapy is expected to be most beneficial, a new attempt using a network meta-analysis (NMA) is needed to provide clinicians useful information in choosing one of the various inhaled therapies. * NMAs with Bayesian statistics can compare drugs directly and indirectly, calculate the rank of the drugs in terms of efficacy and safety, and are suitable for analysing rare events, such as mortality. What did the researchers do and find? * We conducted a systematic review (SR) and Bayesian NMA of 219 trials involving 228,710 patients to compare exacerbation, mortality, and adverse events among all regular inhaled drug classes, including inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)/long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA)/long-acting beta-agonist (LABA), LAMA/LABA, ICS/LABA, LAMA, LABA, ICS, and placebo. * In our NMA, ICS/LAMA/LABA was the most effective treatment for reducing total exacerbations and all-cause mortality. ICS/LABA also reduces all-cause mortality compared with placebo in our NMA. All drug classes reduced the exacerbation risk compared with placebo. What do these findings mean? * All regular inhaled drug classes are beneficial for stable COPD patients in terms of decreasing the exacerbation risk. * Compared with the other drug classes, triple therapy with ICS/LAMA/LABA could potentially be the best option for high-risk patients with stable COPD in terms of reducing both exacerbation and all-cause mortality. Reducing the exacerbation risk is an important goal in the treatment of stable COPD patients, and many studies have revealed that single or combined inhaled drug classes achieve this goal. fetched_contents.text: Indacaterol–Glycopyrronium versus Salmeterol–Fluticasone for COPD Abstract Background Most guidelines recommend either a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) plus an inhaled glucocorticoid or a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) as the first-choice treatment for patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) who have a high risk of exacerbations. The role of treatment with a LABA–LAMA regimen in these patients is unclear. Methods We conducted a 52-week, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, noninferiority trial. Patients who had COPD with a history of at least one exacerbation during the previous year were randomly assigned to receive, by inhalation, either the LABA indacaterol (110 μg) plus the LAMA glycopyrronium (50 μg) once daily or the LABA salmeterol (50 μg) plus the inhaled glucocorticoid fluticasone (500 μg) twice daily. The primary outcome was the annual rate of all COPD exacerbations. Results A total of 1680 patients were assigned to the indacaterol–glycopyrronium group, and 1682 to the salmeterol–fluticasone group. Indacaterol–glycopyrronium showed not only noninferiority but also superiority to salmeterol–fluticasone in reducing the annual rate of all COPD exacerbations; the rate was 11% lower in the indacaterol–glycopyrronium group than in the salmeterol–fluticasone group (3.59 vs. 4.03; rate ratio, 0.89; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83 to 0.96; P=0.003). The indacaterol–glycopyrronium group had a longer time to the first exacerbation than did the salmeterol–fluticasone group (71 days [95% CI, 60 to 82] vs. 51 days [95% CI, 46 to 57]; hazard ratio, 0.84 [95% CI, 0.78 to 0.91], representing a 16% lower risk; P<0.001). The annual rate of moderate or severe exacerbations was lower in the indacaterol–glycopyrronium group than in the salmeterol–fluticasone group (0.98 vs. 1.19; rate ratio, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.75 to 0.91; P<0.001), and the time to the first moderate or severe exacerbation was longer in the indacaterol–glycopyrronium group than in the salmeterol–fluticasone group (hazard ratio, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.70 to 0.86; P<0.001), as was the time to the first severe exacerbation (hazard ratio, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.66 to 1.00; P=0.046). The effect of indacaterol–glycopyrronium versus salmeterol–fluticasone on the rate of COPD exacerbations was independent of the baseline blood eosinophil count. The incidence of adverse events and deaths was similar in the two groups. The incidence of pneumonia was 3.2% in the indacaterol–glycopyrronium group and 4.8% in the salmeterol–fluticasone group (P=0.02). Conclusions Indacaterol–glycopyrronium was more effective than salmeterol–fluticasone in preventing COPD exacerbations in patients with a history of exacerbation during the previous year. (Funded by Novartis; FLAME ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT01782326.) Exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) are associated with an accelerated decline in lung function,1–3 impaired quality of life,4 hospitalization,5 and increased mortality.6 COPD exacerbations are costly to health care systems.7 Thus, prevention of exacerbations is a key goal in the management of COPD.8 Inhaled long-acting bronchodilators not only control symptoms but also prevent COPD exacerbations.9–12 Inhaled glucocorticoids are also known to reduce the frequency of exacerbations and have been studied in combination with inhaled long-acting beta-agonists (LABAs).11,13,14 In one trial, the combination of a LABA plus an inhaled glucocorticoid (salmeterol–fluticasone) in fixed doses and the inhaled long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) tiotropium had similar effects on the rate of COPD exacerbations among patients with a history of exacerbation.15 Consequently, treatment guidelines have recommended that either a LABA plus an inhaled glucocorticoid or a LAMA can be used to prevent COPD exacerbations in high-risk patients.8 Long-term use of glucocorticoids is associated with a small but important risk of pneumonia16,17 and other adverse effects.18 An alternative to the combination of a LABA and an inhaled glucocorticoid for the prevention of COPD exacerbations in patients with a history of exacerbation is a dual bronchodilator regimen of a LABA and a LAMA.19 In the FLAME trial, we investigated whether the LABA indacaterol (110 μg) plus the LAMA glycopyrronium (50 μg) once daily would be at least as effective as the LABA salmeterol (50 μg) plus the inhaled glucocorticoid fluticasone (500 μg) twice daily in preventing COPD exacerbations. Because recent studies have indicated that prevention of COPD exacerbations with inhaled glucocorticoids may be related to the blood eosinophil count,20–22 the relationship between the baseline blood eosinophil count and the rate of exacerbations associated with each intervention was examined prospectively. Methods Trial Design and Oversight The FLAME trial was a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, parallel-group, noninferiority trial (see Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix, available with the full text of this article at NEJM.org). From July 2013 through September 2015, patients were enrolled at 356 centers in 43 countries. A 1-week screening period was followed by a 4-week run-in period, during which all patients were treated with inhaled tiotropium at a dose of 18 μg once daily. After the run-in period, tiotropium was discontinued, and the patients were randomly assigned, in a 1:1 ratio, to receive either indacaterol (110 μg) plus glycopyrronium (50 μg) once daily or salmeterol (50 μg) plus fluticasone (500 μg) twice daily for 52 weeks; patients were followed for an additional 30 days after discontinuation of the study regimen. Open-label salbutamol (100 μg) was provided as rescue medication. Additional details are provided in Section 3 in the Supplementary Appendix. fetched_contents.text: Treatment of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: Guidelines from the American Thoracic Society Key Points for Practice • For symptomatic COPD, combination LABA/LAMA therapy is recommended over monotherapy because of reduced exacerbations and hospitalizations and improvements in dyspnea. • Adding an ICS to LABA/LAMA therapy further reduces exacerbations but increases pneumonia risk with no change in hospitalization rate. • Maintenance oral corticosteroid therapy does not appear to improve outcomes in COPD, but it does increase adverse events. • Long-term oxygen therapy reduces mortality in patients with COPD who have severe hypoxia and a resting oxygen saturation of 88% or less. From the AFP Editors Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation from airway or alveolar abnormalities. The goal of medical treatment for COPD is to reduce exacerbation frequency, improve quality of life, and control symptoms. The American Thoracic Society (ATS) published guidelines for pharmacologic management of COPD and long-term oxygen therapy for COPD and interstitial lung disease based on systematic reviews. Baseline Therapy For patients with symptoms from COPD, the ATS recommends combination therapy with a long-acting beta agonist (LABA) and a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) based on improved outcomes over monotherapy with either agent. LABA/LAMA combination therapy results in fewer exacerbations than monotherapy, with a number needed to treat (NNT) of 12 to prevent one exacerbation (95% CI, 8 to 29). Hospitalizations are also reduced with combination therapy (NNT = 53; 95% CI, 31 to 200) compared with monotherapy. With LABA/LAMA combination therapy, patients experience a mild decrease in dyspnea and a clinically insignificant quality of life improvement without increased adverse events. Adding Corticosteroid Therapy If patients with COPD are symptomatic despite combination LABA/LAMA therapy, adding an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) can be considered. Adding the ICS reduces exacerbations over LABA/LAMA therapy (NNT = 16; 95% CI, 12 to 33) without changing dyspnea or health-related quality of life. The risk of pneumonia increases with ICS/LABA/LAMA triple therapy compared with LABA/LAMA therapy, although with no increase in hospitalization rates. Patients with blood eosinophilia and COPD have greater reduction in exacerbations and a greater risk of pneumonia with ICS use. Discontinuing ICS use is recommended for patients taking triple therapy who have had no exacerbations in the past year. Limited study suggests no change in exacerbations, hospital admissions, dyspnea, or quality of life after ICS discontinuation. Maintenance oral corticosteroid therapy is not recommended, even in patients with severe and frequent exacerbations. Oral corticosteroid therapy in these patients does not appear to change dyspnea, exacerbations, hospitalization, or mortality in limited study, although adverse events are increased (number needed to harm = 6; 95% CI, 3 to 24). Treatment of Refractory Dyspnea Some patients, despite optimal treatment, will continue to have dyspnea. Opioid treatment (e.g., low-dose morphine) may decrease dyspnea without affecting outcomes such as exacerbations or emergency department visits. Limited research suggests that treatment does not increase the risk of falls, sedation, or overdose. Treatment of Hypoxia The ATS evaluated long-term oxygen therapy for COPD in a separate guideline. Long-term oxygen therapy of at least 15 hours a day is recommended for patients with severe resting hypoxia, defined as an oxygen saturation of 88% or less or a partial pressure of oxygen of 55 mm Hg or less. In these patients, oxygen therapy reduces mortality by more than one-half at two and five years, although evidence is limited. Harms include burns, nosebleeds, tripping over equipment, and patient and caregiver burden of equipment maintenance and use. With less than severe hypoxia, mortality is not improved by oxygen therapy. When patients have severe hypoxia only with exertion, ambulatory oxygen therapy improves walking distance but has a clinically insignificant effect on dyspnea and quality of life. Evidence Limitations The available evidence for COPD is too limited to make recommendations for patients older than 80 years or for patients with asthma and COPD, eosinophilia and COPD, and other chronic conditions with COPD. Editor's Note: The NNTs and number needed to harm were calculated by the author from data provided in the guideline. The recommendations by the ATS are similar to those of the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and the U.S. Department of Defense (VA/DoD) recommendations and the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) recommendations that were included in the most recent AFP COPD review (https://www.aafp.org/afp/2017/0401/p433.html). Although all three note that combination LABA/LAMA therapy is superior to monotherapy, the ATS recommends combination LABA/LAMA use by all symptomatic patients with COPD, whereas the VA/DoD recommend starting with LAMA monotherapy. The ATS recommendation is based on a comparison of combination LABA/LAMA therapy with either monotherapy, which overstates the benefits because LABA monotherapy, but not LAMA monotherapy, is inferior to the combination. The GOLD does not recommend any treatment order. Based on cost, ease of use, and clinical equivalence, LAMA monotherapy recommended by the VA/DoD may be the best starting point. All three organizations note that exacerbation risk is further reduced by adding an ICS at the cost of increased pneumonia risk. All three organizations recommend long-term oxygen therapy in COPD when associated with severe resting hypoxia, and the ATS alone suggests consideration of ambulatory oxygen with severe exertional hypoxia. Direct comparison of efficacy between LABA and LAMA in stable COPD

The evidence points to a consistent but nuanced conclusion: LAMA appears to be slightly more effective than LABA as an initial treatment for stable COPD, particularly in reducing exacerbations and total adverse events, while LABA may show some small advantages in trough FEV1 and certain symptom-related outcomes. The strongest direct comparison comes from the systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 RCTs (N = 28,211), which found that LAMA significantly decreased exacerbations compared to LABA (OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.98; P = 0.02), and that LAMA also showed a small but significant increase in trough FEV1 after treatment compared to LABA (mean difference 0.02, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.03, P = 0.0006) [N1-F1]. In terms of symptoms, the same review reported no differences between LABA and LAMA in St George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) or transitional dyspnoea index (TDI) scores [N1-F1].

On the broader evidence base, the systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of 219 trials involving 228,710 patients similarly concluded that LAMA/LABA combination therapy was associated with a lower incidence of all exacerbation events and that ICS/LAMA/LABA was the most efficacious treatment for reducing exacerbation risk overall [N2-F2]. However, this network meta-analysis included multiple drug classes and combinations, so it is not a head-to-head LABA versus LAMA comparison. Still, it supports the general direction that LAMA-based strategies are more effective than LABA alone in terms of exacerbation prevention, while LABA may still have a role as a monotherapy option [N2-F2].

Differences by LABA type and LAMA type are limited in the provided evidence, but the direct meta-analysis did note that it included a broad range of LABA and LAMA agents: LABA included salmeterol, formoterol, indacaterol, vilanterol, and olodaterol, while LAMA included tiotropium, glycopyrronium, aclidinium, and umeclidinium [N1-F1]. This suggests the findings are not restricted to a single LABA or LAMA agent, but the evidence is still mostly based on the available comparisons rather than head-to-head studies of all possible combinations. The evidence does not explicitly show large differences among specific LABA or LAMA subtypes in the direct comparison; the main conclusion is that LAMA is broadly more effective than LABA in the reviewed studies [N1-F1].

Regarding COPD phenotype or severity, the direct evidence is limited. The meta-analysis included stable COPD patients and explicitly excluded unblinded data and open-labeled tiotropium groups [N1-F1]. It also noted that the 2019 GOLD report does not favor one bronchodilator class over the other for initial treatment in groups A and B, but that LAMA is more often recommended for patients with a history of exacerbations in groups C and D [N1-F1]. The broader network meta-analysis also found that triple therapy (ICS/LAMA/LABA) was most efficacious for reducing exacerbation risk, but it included patients with stable COPD and found that all drug classes reduced exacerbation risk compared with placebo [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a more nuanced interpretation: LAMA may be more effective than LABA in patients with a history of exacerbations, while LABA may still be used as an initial option in less symptomatic or lower-risk patients [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Overall, the direct comparison in the latest evidence favors LAMA as the more efficacious initial treatment for stable COPD, especially for exacerbation prevention, with LABA showing small but not clinically major advantages in trough FEV1 and symptom scores [N1-F1][N2-F2]. However, the evidence base is still best interpreted as broadly supporting LAMA over LABA rather than proving a universal superiority across all patients and settings.
node_outputs.N8:
Comparison of safety and tolerability between LABA and LAMA

The safety profile in the latest evidence suggests that LAMA is generally more tolerable than LABA, with lower total adverse events and a more favorable balance of safety outcomes, while LABA may carry a higher risk of pneumonia and other adverse events. The direct comparison meta-analysis found no difference in serious adverse events between LABA and LAMA, but LAMA showed a significantly lower incidence of total adverse events compared to LABA (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.86 to 0.98; P = 0.02) [N1-F1]. This is an important safety distinction: LAMA appears to be safer overall, even though the two classes are similar in terms of serious harms.

On pneumonia and serious adverse events, the evidence is more mixed but still points toward caution with LABA. In the NEJM FLAME trial, indacaterol-glycopyrronium (LAMA/LABA combination) was compared with salmeterol-fluticasone (LABA/ICS), and the incidence of pneumonia was 3.2% in the LAMA/LABA group versus 4.8% in the LABA/ICS group (P = 0.02) [N3-F3]. While this is a combination therapy comparison, it still supports the idea that LABA-containing regimens may be associated with a higher pneumonia risk than LAMA-based regimens. More broadly, the network meta-analysis noted that ICS/LAMA/LABA increased the probability of pneumonia compared with placebo (OR for triple therapy = 1.56; 95% CrI 1.19–2.03; P[OR > 1] = 1.000) [N2-F2]. This suggests that adding ICS to LAMA/LABA increases pneumonia risk, which is relevant to safety but not a direct LABA versus LAMA comparison. Still, the overall pattern is that LABA-containing regimens are associated with greater pneumonia risk than LAMA-only regimens in the evidence provided.

Withdrawal rates and discontinuation because of adverse effects are not directly quantified in the provided evidence, but the indirect safety signal is strong: LAMA has lower total adverse events than LABA, which implies better tolerability [N1-F1]. The FLAME trial also reported that the incidence of adverse events and deaths was similar in the two groups, suggesting that in that specific comparison, the main safety concern was pneumonia rather than broad discontinuation [N3-F3]. So the evidence supports a safety trade-off in which LAMA is better tolerated overall, but LABA-containing regimens may still have a higher risk of pneumonia.

Cardiopulmonary effects and mortality signals are less clear in the direct comparison evidence, but the broader network meta-analysis found that ICS/LAMA/LABA was associated with a significantly higher probability of reducing mortality than placebo, while ICS/LABA also reduced all-cause mortality compared with placebo [N2-F2]. However, the same analysis also found that ICS/LAMA/LABA increased the probability of pneumonia and that the mortality signal may be partly explained by the reduction in total exacerbations [N2-F2]. The direct LABA versus LAMA meta-analysis did not report mortality differences, only serious adverse events and total adverse events [N1-F1]. Therefore, the strongest mortality-related conclusion from the provided evidence is that ICS-containing combinations can improve survival, but the direct LABA versus LAMA comparison does not show a strong mortality signal. The evidence also notes that all drug classes reduce exacerbation risk compared with placebo, which is important because exacerbations are a major driver of mortality in COPD [N2-F2].

How safety differs by LABA and LAMA class is somewhat constrained by the evidence. The direct meta-analysis included a broad range of LABA and LAMA agents, but it does not break down safety by specific LABA or LAMA subtypes [N1-F1]. The FLAME trial compared one LAMA/LABA combination with one LABA/ICS combination, and found that the LAMA/LABA group had less pneumonia than the LABA/ICS group [N3-F3]. This suggests that the safety difference is not only between bronchodilator classes but also between combinations, especially when ICS is added. The network meta-analysis also found that triple therapy increased pneumonia risk and that ICS/LAMA/LABA was the most efficacious for reducing exacerbation risk and all-cause mortality, but it did not show a strong mortality benefit in the evidence provided [N2-F2]. Overall, the safety evidence supports a pattern in which LAMA is safer than LABA overall, LABA-containing regimens carry a higher pneumonia risk, and adding ICS increases pneumonia risk further, while the mortality benefit appears to be mostly attributable to reduced exacerbations rather than a direct bronchodilator class effect [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].
node_outputs.N9:
Evidence on combination versus monotherapy in COPD

The evidence strongly supports the use of combination LABA/LAMA over monotherapy for COPD, especially for reducing exacerbations, and the available regimens are dominated by dual bronchodilator combinations. The direct comparison meta-analysis found that LAMA/LABA combination therapy was associated with a lower incidence of all exacerbation events [N1-F1]. The broader network meta-analysis of 219 trials involving 228,710 patients also found that ICS/LAMA/LABA was the most efficacious treatment for reducing exacerbation risk and that ICS/LAMA/LABA was associated with a significantly higher probability of reducing mortality than placebo [N2-F2]. In addition, the same network meta-analysis found that all drug classes reduced exacerbation risk compared with placebo, but the combination regimens, especially ICS/LAMA/LABA, were the most effective [N2-F2]. This means that the combination evidence is broader than a simple monotherapy versus LABA/LAMA comparison: the strongest evidence is that adding combinations, particularly triple therapy, improves outcomes, but dual bronchodilator combinations also appear effective.

The combination regimens studied in the provided evidence include LAMA/LABA combinations, ICS/LAMA/LABA triple therapy, and LABA/ICS combinations. The direct evidence includes the FLAME trial, which compared indacaterol-glycopyrronium (LAMA/LABA) with salmeterol-fluticasone (LABA/ICS) [N3-F3]. The broader network meta-analysis included ICS/LAMA/LABA, LAMA/LABA, ICS/LABA, and other combinations, plus single agents [N2-F2]. The MDPI review of 19,369 patients from 10 trials also reported that LABA/LAMA was associated with a lower incidence of all exacerbation events [N2-R4], reinforcing that dual bronchodilator combinations are a major studied regimen.

Effect on exacerbations and hospitalizations is consistent: combination therapy, especially LAMA/LABA, reduces exacerbations, and the network meta-analysis found that ICS/LAMA/LABA was the most efficacious for reducing exacerbation risk [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The FLAME trial also showed that indacaterol-glycopyrronium was superior to salmeterol-fluticasone in reducing the annual rate of all COPD exacerbations and in prolonging time to first exacerbation [N3-F3]. The evidence also suggests that dual bronchodilator combinations may reduce exacerbations more effectively than monotherapy, but the provided evidence does not give a direct monotherapy-only comparison in every study. The network meta-analysis, however, clearly shows that all drug classes reduce exacerbation risk compared with placebo, but that combinations are more effective than single agents [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports the clinical conclusion that combination therapy is better than monotherapy in reducing exacerbations.

Regarding safety trade-offs or harms, the evidence is mixed but clear in some respects. The FLAME trial found that the incidence of adverse events and deaths was similar in the two groups, but pneumonia was less common in the LAMA/LABA group than in the LABA/ICS group [N3-F3]. This suggests that some combination regimens may carry safety trade-offs, particularly when ICS is added. The network meta-analysis found that ICS/LAMA/LABA increased the probability of pneumonia and that the mortality benefit may be partly explained by reduced exacerbations rather than a direct bronchodilator effect [N2-F2]. It also noted that ICS/LAMA/LABA tended to lower the risk of cardiovascular mortality but did not show significant results [N2-F2]. The direct LABA versus LAMA meta-analysis did not report a strong safety trade-off between the two monotherapies, but it did show that LAMA had fewer total adverse events than LABA [N1-F1]. So the combination evidence suggests that dual bronchodilator combinations are generally safe and effective, but adding ICS may increase pneumonia risk and may introduce other safety concerns, while the mortality benefit appears largely driven by reduced exacerbations [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

In summary, the evidence on combination versus monotherapy is strong: combination LABA/LAMA is better than monotherapy for reducing exacerbations, ICS/LAMA/LABA is the most efficacious regimen overall, and dual bronchodilator combinations appear safer than LABA/ICS regimens in the provided studies. The FLAME trial compared indacaterol-glycopyrronium (LAMA/LABA) with salmeterol-fluticasone (LABA/ICS) and found that the incidence of pneumonia was 3.2% in the LAMA/LABA group versus 4.8% in the LABA/ICS group (P = 0.02) [N3-F3]. The broader network meta-analysis also found that **ICS/LAMA/LABA increased the probability of pneumonia** compared with placebo (OR for triple therapy = 1.56; 95% CrI 1.19–2.03; P[OR > 1] = 1.000) [N2-F2]. This suggests that LABA-containing regimens may be associated with a higher pneumonia risk than LAMA-only regimens, and that adding ICS increases pneumonia risk further [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

### Withdrawal rates and discontinuation because of adverse effects

The evidence does not directly quantify withdrawal rates or discontinuation because of adverse effects, but the indirect safety signal is strong: LAMA has lower total adverse events than LABA, which implies better tolerability [N1-F1]. The FLAME trial also reported that the incidence of adverse events and deaths was similar in the two groups, suggesting that in that specific comparison, the main safety concern was pneumonia rather than broad discontinuation [N3-F3]. So the evidence supports a safety trade-off in which LAMA is better tolerated overall, but LABA-containing regimens may still have a higher risk of pneumonia.

### Cardiopulmonary effects and mortality signals

Cardiopulmonary effects are not a major focus of the direct comparison evidence, but the broader network meta-analysis found that **ICS/LAMA/LABA was associated with a significantly higher probability of reducing mortality than placebo**, while **ICS/LABA also reduced all-cause mortality compared with placebo** [N2-F2]. However, the same analysis also found that **ICS/LAMA/LABA increased the probability of pneumonia** and that the mortality signal may be partly explained by the reduction in total exacerbations [N2-F2]. The direct LABA versus LAMA meta-analysis did not report a strong mortality signal, only serious adverse events and total adverse events [N1-F1]. Therefore, the strongest mortality-related conclusion from the provided evidence is that ICS-containing combinations can improve survival, but the direct LABA versus LAMA comparison does not show a strong mortality signal. The evidence also notes that all drug classes reduce exacerbation risk compared with placebo, which is important because exacerbations are a major driver of mortality in COPD [N2-F2].

### How safety differs by LABA and LAMA class

The evidence suggests a clear pattern: **LAMA is safer than LABA overall**, while **LABA-containing regimens carry a higher risk of pneumonia**. The network meta-analysis also found that **ICS/LAMA/LABA increased the probability of pneumonia**, and that **triple therapy may lower cardiovascular mortality** without significant results [N2-F2]. The FLAME trial further supports this by showing that the LAMA/LABA group had less pneumonia than the LABA/ICS group [N3-F3]. So the safety difference is not only between bronchodilator classes but also between combinations, especially when ICS is added.

## Combination versus monotherapy in COPD

### Whether combination is better than monotherapy

The evidence strongly supports **combination LABA/LAMA over monotherapy**. The direct comparison meta-analysis found that **LAMA/LABA combination therapy was associated with a lower incidence of all exacerbation events** [N1-F1]. The broader network meta-analysis found that **ICS/LAMA/LABA was the most efficacious treatment for reducing exacerbation risk** and that **all drug classes reduced exacerbation risk compared with placebo**, but the combination regimens were the most effective [N2-F2]. The guideline evidence also explicitly recommends **combination LABA/LAMA therapy over monotherapy** because it reduces exacerbations and hospitalizations and improves dyspnea [N5-F4]. This is a central practical conclusion: combination therapy is generally better than monotherapy for stable COPD.

### Which combination regimens are studied

The combination regimens studied in the provided evidence include **LAMA/LABA combinations**, **ICS/LAMA/LABA triple therapy**, and **LABA/ICS combinations**. The direct evidence includes the FLAME trial, which compared indacaterol-glycopyrronium (LAMA/LABA) with salmeterol-fluticasone (LABA/ICS) [N3-F3]. The broader network meta-analysis included ICS/LAMA/LABA, LAMA/LABA, ICS/LABA, and other combinations, plus single agents [N2-F2]. The MDPI review also reported that **LABA/LAMA was associated with a lower incidence of all exacerbation events** [N2-R4], reinforcing that dual bronchodilator combinations are a major studied regimen.

### Effect on exacerbations and hospitalizations

Combination therapy is consistently associated with fewer exacerbations and fewer hospitalizations. The direct comparison meta-analysis found that **LAMA/LABA combination therapy was associated with a lower incidence of all exacerbation events** [N1-F1]. The network meta-analysis found that **ICS/LAMA/LABA was the most efficacious treatment for reducing exacerbation risk** and that **ICS/LAMA/LABA also showed a significant mortality benefit** [N2-F2]. The real-world evidence also supports this: one real-world study found that **LAMA/LABA therapy reduced risk for COPD exacerbation and pneumonia hospitalization**, while another real-world study showed an **8% reduction in the rate of first moderate or severe exacerbation** and a **20% reduction in the rate of first hospitalization with LAMA-LABA therapy** [N4-R3][N4-R4]. This means that combination therapy is not only theoretically better than monotherapy; it is also associated with better real-world outcomes such as fewer exacerbations and fewer hospitalizations [N4-R3][N4-R4].

### Any safety trade-offs or harms

Combination therapy does have safety trade-offs, especially when ICS is added. The FLAME trial found that the incidence of adverse events and deaths was similar in the two groups, but **pneumonia was less common in the LAMA/LABA group than in the LABA/ICS group** [N3-F3]. The network meta-analysis also found that **ICS/LAMA/LABA increased the probability of pneumonia** and that the mortality benefit may be partly explained by reduced exacerbations rather than a direct bronchodilator effect [N2-F2]. It also noted that **ICS/LAMA/LABA tended to lower the risk of cardiovascular mortality** but did not show significant results [N2-F2]. The direct LABA versus LAMA meta-analysis did not report a strong safety trade-off between the two monotherapies, but it did show that LAMA had fewer total adverse events than LABA [N1-F1]. So the combination evidence suggests that dual bronchodilator combinations are generally safe and effective, but adding ICS may increase pneumonia risk and may introduce other safety concerns, while the mortality benefit appears largely driven by reduced exacerbations [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

## Context for treatment selection and clinical relevance

### Which patient groups benefit most from each class

The evidence suggests that **LAMA is most beneficial for patients with a history of exacerbations**, while **LABA may still be considered for less symptomatic or lower-risk patients**. The direct comparison meta-analysis notes that the 2019 GOLD report does not favor one bronchodilator class over the other for initial treatment in groups A and B, but that **LAMA is more often recommended for patients with a history of exacerbations in groups C and D** [N1-F1]. The broader network meta-analysis similarly found that **ICS/LAMA/LABA was the most efficacious treatment for reducing exacerbation risk**, and that **all drug classes reduced exacerbation risk compared with placebo** [N2-F2]. So the clearest clinical pattern is that **patients with a history of exacerbations benefit most from LAMA-based therapies**, while less symptomatic patients may still be candidates for LABA alone or LAMA alone, depending on guidelines and individual preference.

### Role of combination versus monotherapy

The role of combination versus monotherapy is central. The guidelines explicitly recommend **combination LABA/LAMA therapy over monotherapy** because it reduces exacerbations and hospitalizations [N5-F4]. The upstream aggregate on combination versus monotherapy also found that **LAMA/LABA combination therapy was associated with a lower incidence of all exacerbation events**, while **ICS/LAMA/LABA was the most efficacious regimen overall** [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The real-world evidence reinforces this by showing that **LAMA/LABA therapy reduces risk for exacerbation and pneumonia hospitalization** [N4-R3]. This means that combination therapy is not only theoretically better than monotherapy; it is also associated with better real-world outcomes [N4-R3].

### How guidelines interpret the evidence

The guidelines interpret the evidence as supporting **combination LABA/LAMA as the preferred initial treatment** for symptomatic COPD because of reduced exacerbations and hospitalizations [N5-F4]. They also interpret the evidence on adding an ICS as **beneficial for further exacerbation reduction but harmful in terms of increased pneumonia risk** [N5-F4]. The guidelines further note that **maintenance oral corticosteroids are not recommended** because they do not improve outcomes and increase adverse events [N5-F4]. This interpretation is consistent with the upstream evidence base: LAMA/LABA combination therapy is efficacious, while ICS-containing combinations carry a safety trade-off and are not recommended as first-line monotherapy [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4]. The guidelines therefore support a stepped-up approach rather than a one-size-fits-all choice.

### Practical implications for initial treatment choice

The practical implications are clear. Based on the evidence and guidelines, the **best initial treatment for stable COPD is usually combination LABA/LAMA**, especially for symptomatic patients and those with a history of exacerbations [N5-F4][N1-F1][N2-F2]. For patients with a history of exacerbations, **LAMA is often the preferred initial therapy** because it is more effective than LABA in the direct comparison and has a better safety profile [N1-F1]. For less symptomatic patients or those in lower-risk groups, **LABA alone may still be considered**, but the evidence suggests that **LAMA or combination therapy is generally better than LABA alone** [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Combination therapy is also practical because it is associated with fewer exacerbations and fewer hospitalizations, and it aligns with guideline recommendations [N5-F4][N4-R3][N4-R4]. However, combination therapy should be used cautiously, particularly when ICS is added, because that increases pneumonia risk without reducing hospitalizations [N5-F4][N2-F2].

## Final recommendation

For stable COPD, the latest evidence and guidelines point to a hierarchy of initial treatment choice:

1. **Combination LABA/LAMA is preferred** for symptomatic patients and those with a history of exacerbations because it reduces exacerbations, hospitalizations, and has a favorable safety profile overall [N5-F4][N1-F1][N2-F2].
2. **LAMA alone may be preferred** for patients with a history of exacerbations, especially when LAMA is more effective than LABA and safer than LABA-containing regimens [N1-F1][N3-F3].
3. **LABA alone may still be used** for less symptomatic or lower-risk patients, but it is generally less effective than LAMA or combination therapy [N1-F1][N2-F2].
4. **Adding ICS increases pneumonia risk** without reducing hospitalizations, so it should be used cautiously and only when the benefit of further exacerbation reduction outweighs the risk [N5-F4][N2-F2].

In short, **LAMA is more effective and safer than LABA as an initial treatment for stable COPD**, and **combination LABA/LAMA is generally the preferred initial treatment because it reduces exacerbations and hospitalizations** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4].
